spixs-macaw.hook: Extinct in the wild, then a small reintroduction: still not a self-sustaining Caatinga population.
spixs-macaw.imageAlt: Two blue Spix’s macaws perched on aviary mesh in a conservation facility
spixs-macaw.what: Spix’s macaw is a small blue parrot endemic to gallery woodland along the São Francisco drainage in Bahia, Brazil. BirdLife / IUCN list it as Extinct in the Wild. The last accepted wild bird disappeared around 2000. Captive flocks in Germany, Brazil, and elsewhere kept the species alive. Releases near Curaçá began in 2022; a few chicks hatched in the wild. The free-flying group has numbered in the low tens and still depends on supplemental feeding: IUCN EW therefore still applies.
spixs-macaw.range: Historically a narrow Caatinga corridor in Bahia. Today: breeding centres plus a contested reintroduction site at Curaçá.
spixs-macaw.story: Trapping for the cage-bird trade and the cutting of caraiba woodland emptied the wild. The 2022-24 releases showed the species can fly and nest again. In 2025 a circovirus outbreak and a breakdown between ICMBio and breeding partners put the tiny wild group at risk. Do not call this a recovered wild population.
spixs-macaw.when: IUCN: Extinct in the Wild. A handful of released birds, not a restored species.
spixs-macaw.humanRole: The pet trade and habitat loss removed it; captivity kept a gene pool; reintroduction is unfinished and fragile.
spixs-macaw.sourcesNote: IUCN / BirdLife (Cyanopsitta spixii, EW); Vercillo et al. 2024 (Diversity) on the Curaçá releases; 2025 press on the circovirus crisis.

woolly-mammoth.hook: A Late Pleistocene giant of the north: climate and people both belong in the ending.
woolly-mammoth.imageAlt: A life-size woolly mammoth reconstruction in a museum gallery
woolly-mammoth.what: The woolly mammoth was a cold-steppe elephant with long hair and curved tusks. It is extinct. Its closest living relative is the Asian elephant. Ancient DNA and dated bones give a clearer timeline than most Ice Age mammals.
woolly-mammoth.range: The mammoth steppe of northern Eurasia and North America. As the Ice Age ended, habitable grassland shrank northward and fragmented.
woolly-mammoth.story: Mainland populations disappeared around 10,000-12,000 years ago, in the same window as other Holarctic megafauna. A dwarfed population on Wrangel Island survived until about 4,000 years ago (around 1650 BCE). Warming that replaced steppe with wet tundra and forest is a major, well-supported cause. Human hunting is also widely cited, and the mix almost certainly varied by region. Claiming a single cause overstates the evidence.
woolly-mammoth.when: Extinct. Mainland: end-Pleistocene. Last island holdouts: mid-Holocene, about 4,000 years ago.
woolly-mammoth.humanRole: Hunting is a widely cited contributing cause alongside climate-driven habitat loss: not a proven sole cause.
woolly-mammoth.sourcesNote: Dated Wrangel remains (Vartanyan and later ancient-DNA studies); reviews of Late Pleistocene megafauna extinction.

scale.lengthLabel: Body length without the trunk and tusks
scale.captionExtra: The last woolly mammoths lived on Wrangel Island in the Arctic Ocean until about 4,000 years ago.

dodo.hook: A flightless pigeon of Mauritius, gone within about a century of permanent European settlement.
dodo.imageAlt: Oxford museum display with a dodo skeleton and a feathered reconstruction
dodo.what: The dodo was a large flightless pigeon endemic to Mauritius. IUCN lists it as Extinct. No complete stuffed specimen survives; knowledge comes from bones, a few relics, and seventeenth-century accounts and paintings.
dodo.range: Mauritius only. It had no mainland population.
dodo.story: Dutch and other visitors hunted dodos. More decisive were the pigs, rats, dogs, and crab-eating macaques people brought, which ate eggs and chicks, plus the cutting of forest. The last widely accepted sighting is 1662; the species was gone by the 1690s.
dodo.when: Extinct by the late seventeenth century, on an island people had only recently occupied year-round.
dodo.humanRole: Hunting plus introduced mammals on an island with no prior land predators.
dodo.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Raphus cucullatus, EX); Roberts & Solow and later reviews of last-sighting dates.

scale.captionExtra: The last confirmed sighting on Mauritius was in 1662, and the species was probably gone by 1690.

sources.label: Natural History Museum, London: The dodo bird, the real facts about this icon of extinction
Tetrapod Zoology, Darren Naish: The Dodo in Life
Nature, Roberts and Solow 2003: When did the dodo become extinct?

passenger-pigeon.hook: Once perhaps the most numerous bird in North America; the last captive bird died in 1914.
passenger-pigeon.imageAlt: A mounted passenger pigeon on museum display
passenger-pigeon.what: The passenger pigeon was a long-tailed migratory pigeon of eastern North American forests. Flocks were so large that nineteenth-century observers described them darkening the sky for hours. IUCN lists it as Extinct.
passenger-pigeon.range: Breeding colonies in the deciduous forests of the eastern and central United States and southern Canada; wintering farther south in the same region.
passenger-pigeon.story: Order-of-magnitude estimates put the pre-collapse population in the billions (often cited as 3-5 billion; the true figure is unknown). Market hunting and the destruction of nesting colonies in the late 1800s broke a species that apparently needed huge colonies to breed. The last wild birds were gone around 1900. Martha, the last captive, died on 1 September 1914 at the Cincinnati Zoo.
passenger-pigeon.when: Extinct. Last captive death dated to the day: 1 September 1914.
passenger-pigeon.humanRole: Industrial hunting and forest clearance: a human-caused extinction with an unusually precise end date.
passenger-pigeon.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Ectopistes migratorius, EX); Cincinnati Zoo record for Martha; Schorger and later historical estimates.

thylacine.hook: The striped marsupial predator of Tasmania: last captive animal died in 1936.
thylacine.imageAlt: Historical photograph of two thylacines in a stone enclosure
thylacine.what: The thylacine, or Tasmanian tiger, was a dog-sized marsupial carnivore with a stiff tail and dark stripes on the back. IUCN lists it as Extinct. It is not a big cat.
thylacine.range: Tasmania at the end. Earlier in the Holocene it also lived on mainland Australia and in New Guinea; those populations were already gone before the colonial hunt in Tasmania.
thylacine.story: After British settlement, Tasmania ran a government bounty on thylacines, blaming them for sheep losses. Habitat clearing, introduced dogs, and possibly disease added pressure. The last captive animal died on 7 September 1936 at Hobart’s Beaumaris Zoo. Later sighting claims have not produced a verified wild animal.
thylacine.humanRole: A state bounty and persecution as a supposed sheep killer, on an island already altered by settlement.
thylacine.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Thylacinus cynocephalus, EX); Beaumaris Zoo record, 1936.

scale.captionExtra: The last known thylacine died at Hobart Zoo in Tasmania in 1936, and the species was declared extinct in 1982.

sources.label: University of Michigan Museum of Zoology, Animal Diversity Web: Thylacinus cynocephalus (Tasmanian wolf)

stellers-sea-cow.hook: Described in 1741; hunted out by 1768: about 27 years after Europeans found it.
stellers-sea-cow.imageAlt: Nineteenth-century scientific illustration of a Steller’s sea cow in side view
stellers-sea-cow.what: Steller’s sea cow was a huge, slow sirenian: a relative of dugongs and manatees: that grazed kelp. IUCN lists it as Extinct. Georg Wilhelm Steller described it during Vitus Bering’s 1741 expedition.
stellers-sea-cow.range: By the time of European contact it survived only around the Commander Islands in the North Pacific. Bones show a wider North Pacific range earlier in the Holocene.
stellers-sea-cow.story: Fur-hunting crews killed the animals for meat, fat, and hide. They were easy to approach. The last were taken in 1768. Climate and earlier Indigenous hunting may have already shrunk the range; the final disappearance is a documented overkill.
stellers-sea-cow.when: Extinct, 1768: one of the fastest recorded wipeouts of a large mammal.
stellers-sea-cow.humanRole: Direct hunting by fur crews after 1741 finished a species already confined to islands.
stellers-sea-cow.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Hydrodamalis gigas, EX); Steller’s 1741 account; 1768 last-kill date in later compilations.

scale.captionExtra: It was discovered in 1741 and hunted to extinction by 1768.

sources.label: Dimensions.com: Steller's sea cow, Hydrodamalis gigas, dimensions and drawings

Natural History Museum, London: Steller's sea cow, the first historical extinction of a marine mammal at human hands

aurochs.hook: The wild ancestor of cattle; the last recorded animal died in Poland in 1627.
aurochs.imageAlt: A reconstruction of a black aurochs bull with forward-curving horns
aurochs.what: The aurochs was a large wild bovine and the principal ancestor of domestic cattle. IUCN lists it as Extinct. Its genes persist in living cows; the wild form does not.
aurochs.range: Europe, much of Asia, and North Africa in the Holocene, after a Late Pleistocene expansion into ice-free land. By the Middle Ages it was already a forest and marshland remnant in Europe.
aurochs.story: Hunting and the conversion of woodland and wetland to farms steadily removed the wild animal. A Polish royal forest at Jaktorów held the last documented herd. The last animal there died in 1627. Later “aurochs” breeding projects produce cattle that look similar; they are not the extinct species returned.
aurochs.humanRole: Hunting and agriculture erased the wild form; domestication kept only a genetic echo.
aurochs.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Bos primigenius, EX); Polish historical record of the 1627 Jaktorów death.

scale.captionExtra: The last known aurochs, a cow, died in the Jaktorów forest in Poland in 1627.

sources.label: Dimensions.com: Auroch, Bos primigenius, dimensions and drawings

great-auk.hook: A flightless North Atlantic seabird; the last confirmed pair was killed in 1844 for a collector.
great-auk.imageAlt: Nineteenth-century engraving of great auks on an icy North Atlantic shore
great-auk.what: The great auk was a large flightless alcid: a northern counterpart to a penguin in habit, not in ancestry. IUCN lists it as Extinct. It nested in dense colonies on a few predator-free islands.
great-auk.range: Coasts and islands of the North Atlantic, from Newfoundland and Greenland to Iceland, the British Isles, and Norway.
great-auk.story: People took great auks for meat, eggs, and down for centuries. As colonies emptied, museums and collectors paid for skins and eggs. The last confirmed pair was killed on 3 June 1844 on Eldey, Iceland. No later record has been accepted.
great-auk.when: Extinct. Last confirmed killing: 3 June 1844, Eldey.
great-auk.humanRole: Hunting for food and then for specimens, including the last known pair.
great-auk.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Pinguinus impennis, EX); Eldey 1844 eyewitness compilations.

caribbean-monk-seal.hook: The only seal native to the Caribbean; last confirmed sighting 1952, declared extinct later.
caribbean-monk-seal.imageAlt: Historical engraving of a Caribbean monk seal lying on a tropical beach
caribbean-monk-seal.what: The Caribbean monk seal was a tropical earless seal of beaches, cays, and reefs. IUCN lists it as Extinct. It is a different species from the surviving Hawaiian and Mediterranean monk seals.
caribbean-monk-seal.range: The Caribbean Sea and Gulf of Mexico, including the Bahamas, the Greater Antilles, Yucatán, and the Florida Keys.
caribbean-monk-seal.story: From the seventeenth century onward, hunters rendered seals for oil. Later, fishers killed remaining animals as competitors. The last confirmed sighting was in 1952 at Serranilla Bank. NOAA concluded the species was extinct in 2008; IUCN assessed it as Extinct in 2013. Searches found no breeding population.
caribbean-monk-seal.when: Extinct. Last confirmed sighting 1952; formal extinction listings 2008 (NOAA) and 2013 (IUCN).
caribbean-monk-seal.humanRole: Oil hunting and later killing around fishing camps: a human-caused extinction in historical time.
caribbean-monk-seal.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Neomonachus tropicalis, EX, 2013); NOAA extinction finding, 2008.

quagga.hook: A South African zebra subspecies shot out in the wild; the last captive mare died in 1883.
quagga.imageAlt: Nineteenth-century photograph of a quagga mare at the London Zoo
quagga.what: The quagga was a subspecies of the plains zebra, brown on the hindquarters and striped on the head and neck. The International Union for Conservation of Nature assesses the species as a whole (Equus quagga) as Near Threatened; the quagga subspecies is extinct. It is known from skins, skulls, and a few photographs of one mare.
quagga.range: The Karoo and southern Highveld of South Africa. It did not occur farther north than other plains zebras.
quagga.story: Settler hunting for meat and hides, and the conversion of grazing to sheep and cattle, removed the wild population in the 1860s-1870s. The last captive mare died on 12 August 1883 at Artis in Amsterdam. A later breeding project uses plains zebras to mimic the coat; it does not resurrect the historical subspecies.
quagga.when: Extinct in the wild by the late 1870s; last captive death 12 August 1883.
quagga.humanRole: Colonial hunting and pasture conversion: a documented human-caused subspecies extinction.
quagga.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Equus quagga; quagga subspecies extinct); Artis record, 1883.

western-black-rhinoceros.hook: A West African black-rhino subspecies declared extinct by IUCN in 2011 after poaching.
western-black-rhinoceros.imageAlt: Museum photograph of a western black rhinoceros skull in side view
western-black-rhinoceros.what: The western black rhinoceros was a subspecies of the black rhino (Diceros bicornis longipes), adapted to the savannas and woodlands of West and west-central Africa. IUCN declared it Extinct in 2011. Living black rhinos belong to other subspecies.
western-black-rhinoceros.range: Historically from Nigeria and Cameroon into Chad and the Central African Republic. By the late twentieth century only a possible remnant remained in northern Cameroon.
western-black-rhinoceros.story: Horn poaching, not a change of Ice Age climate, ended this subspecies. Surveys in the 2000s failed to find surviving animals; the last accepted sightings were in the mid-2000s. IUCN’s 2011 assessment is the formal extinction listing. Photographs of living longipes individuals are scarce; museum skulls are the clear record.
western-black-rhinoceros.when: IUCN Extinct, 2011. Last accepted wild records: mid-2000s, northern Cameroon.
western-black-rhinoceros.humanRole: The horn trade: a twenty-first-century subspecies extinction.
western-black-rhinoceros.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Diceros bicornis longipes, EX, 2011).

baiji.hook: The Yangtze river dolphin: no confirmed sighting since 2002; IUCN still says possibly extinct.
baiji.imageAlt: Scientific illustration of a baiji, a long-beaked river dolphin, on a dark background
baiji.what: The baiji was a long-beaked freshwater dolphin of the Yangtze. A 2006 range-wide survey found none, and the species is widely treated as functionally extinct. IUCN still lists it as Critically Endangered (Possibly Extinct), not as formal EX, because a last individual cannot be ruled out with certainty.
baiji.range: The middle and lower Yangtze River, China. It did not occur at sea.
baiji.story: Rolling-hook fisheries, ship strikes, dams, and pollution removed quiet water. The last confirmed sighting is 2002. The 2006 expedition is the main basis for calling the species gone. This entry sits in Extinct because the animal is missing from the river; the IUCN code is the more cautious one.
baiji.when: Last confirmed 2002. Functionally extinct after the 2006 survey; IUCN CR (Possibly Extinct).
baiji.humanRole: Industrial use of the Yangtze: bycatch, traffic, and dams: left no room for a river dolphin.
baiji.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Lipotes vexillifer, CR Possibly Extinct); Turvey et al. 2006 survey.

moa.hook: New Zealand’s giant flightless birds, gone within about two centuries of human arrival.
moa.imageAlt: 1867 museum photograph of a mounted giant moa skeleton
moa.what: Moa were several species of large flightless palaeognath birds, unique to New Zealand. This entry uses the South Island giant moa (Dinornis robustus) as the face of the group. All moa are extinct. They had no mammalian land predators before people.
moa.range: New Zealand only. Giant Dinornis species on the North and South Islands; smaller moa in other habitats. None reached Australia or the wider Pacific.
moa.story: Polynesian settlers (the ancestors of Māori) reached New Zealand in the thirteenth century. Dated bones and archaeological sites show moa hunting and large-scale burning of forest. Extinction of the group falls around the fourteenth-fifteenth centuries: commonly summarised as within about 150-200 years of settlement (Holdaway & Jacomb 2000 and later dating). Climate at that moment was not a comparable new shock.
moa.when: Extinct by about the 1400s, after human colonisation: not a deep-time disappearance.
moa.humanRole: Overhunting and firing of forest by the first people on islands with naive megafauna.
moa.sourcesNote: Holdaway & Jacomb 2000 and later radiocarbon syntheses; museum records for Dinornis robustus.

irish-elk.hook: A giant deer of Ice Age Eurasia: gone from Ireland with a cold snap, last holdouts in Siberia in the mid-Holocene.
irish-elk.imageAlt: Mounted skeleton of an Irish elk with enormous palmate antlers
irish-elk.what: The Irish elk, or giant deer, was not an elk. It was a cervid whose males carried the largest antlers of any deer: spans of about 3.5 metres. It is extinct. The famous Irish bog skeletons are the best-known fossils; the living range was far wider than Ireland.
irish-elk.range: Temperate Eurasia in the Late Pleistocene, from Ireland and western Europe to Siberia. Ireland holds many complete skeletons from peat.
irish-elk.story: The Irish population disappeared around the Younger Dryas cold snap, before people settled the island: a climate-driven local extinction. The species then survived in the Urals and western Siberia into the Holocene. The youngest well-dated bones are about 7,700 years old (Stuart et al. 2004). Closing forest and, possibly, growing Neolithic hunting pressure are both discussed for that last range. A single cause is not proven.
irish-elk.when: Extinct. Ireland: end-Pleistocene. Last dated Siberian remains: about 7,700 years ago.
irish-elk.humanRole: Not the cause in Ice Age Ireland. A possible contributing cause in the last Siberian populations, alongside habitat change: a debate, not a verdict.
irish-elk.sourcesNote: Stuart et al. 2004 (Nature) on Holocene survival; later radiocarbon syntheses for Megaloceros giganteus.

smilodon.hook: The La Brea sabertooth of North America: extinct with other American megafauna after people arrived.
smilodon.imageAlt: Life-size museum reconstruction of a Smilodon fatalis standing in a gallery
smilodon.what: Smilodon fatalis was a robust saber-toothed cat of Pleistocene North America, famous from the Rancho La Brea tar pits. It is extinct. It is not a tiger. A larger South American species, S. populator, died out in the same window.
smilodon.range: Western and southern North America in the Late Pleistocene. Close relatives occupied South America.
smilodon.story: The last Smilodon date to about 13,000-10,000 years ago, with other large American mammals. People reached the Americas in the same broad interval (~15,000-10,000 years ago). Hunting of prey, possible hunting of the cats, and climate-driven change in grassland and megafauna communities are all cited. The pattern is first-contact loss of large-mammal genera: not “90 percent of all animals.”
smilodon.when: Extinct at the end of the Pleistocene, about 13,000-10,000 years ago.
smilodon.humanRole: Widely cited as a contributing cause on a newly peopled continent, together with climate and prey collapse: not a proven sole cause.
smilodon.sourcesNote: Rancho La Brea chronology; reviews of North American end-Pleistocene megafauna extinction (e.g. Barnosky, Koch).

megatherium.hook: An elephant-sized South American sloth; butchered bones show people hunted it before it vanished.
megatherium.imageAlt: Mounted Megatherium americanum skeleton in a natural-history museum
megatherium.what: Megatherium americanum was a giant ground sloth of the South American Pleistocene, standing taller than a person when rearing and weighing several tonnes. It is extinct. It browsed and grazed; it was not a tree sloth.
megatherium.range: Temperate South America, especially the Pampas and neighbouring regions of Argentina and Uruguay.
megatherium.story: The species disappeared near the Pleistocene-Holocene boundary. At Campo Laborde, Argentina, bones with cut marks date to about 12,600 calendar years ago (Politis and later redating): direct evidence that people butchered Megatherium. Climate was also shifting. The American megafaunal pulse is the loss of large-mammal genera after first human arrival, not a wipeout of all fauna.
megatherium.when: Extinct around 12,000-10,000 years ago; hunted in the late Pleistocene.
megatherium.humanRole: Hunting is archaeologically attested. Climate change is a co-cause in the wider South American extinction pulse.
megatherium.sourcesNote: Campo Laborde butchery dates (Politis et al.); reviews of South American megafauna extinction.

thylacoleo.hook: Australia’s largest marsupial carnivore: gone in the same 50-40 thousand-year window as the rest of the continent’s megafauna.
thylacoleo.imageAlt: Fossil skull of a marsupial lion showing the huge slicing premolars
thylacoleo.what: Thylacoleo carnifex, the marsupial lion, was a leopard- to lion-sized predator with enormous slicing premolars. It is extinct. It is a wombat relative, not a cat.
thylacoleo.range: Pleistocene Australia, in woodland and open country. Cave deposits record it across much of the continent.
thylacoleo.story: Australian megafauna: genera of large mammals, reptiles, and birds: disappeared around 50,000-40,000 years ago, after people reached Sahul (~65,000-50,000). A continent-wide dating study put the pulse near 46,000 years ago (Roberts et al. 2001). Climate is discussed; the Last Glacial Maximum itself is too late to be the sole cause. The human role is central in most recent syntheses and still debated in detail.
thylacoleo.when: Extinct about 46,000-40,000 years ago, with Australian megafauna.
thylacoleo.humanRole: Arrival of people is the leading cited cause, with climate as a possible co-factor: not a proven single mechanism.
thylacoleo.sourcesNote: Roberts et al. 2001 (Science) on ~46 ka extinction; later Australian megafauna reviews.

diprotodon.hook: The largest marsupial ever: a rhino-sized browser of Pleistocene Australia, gone with the rest of the megafauna.
diprotodon.imageAlt: Scientific reconstruction of a Diprotodon standing in dry grassland
diprotodon.what: Diprotodon optatum was the largest known marsupial, a bulky browser about the size of a rhinoceros. It is extinct. Trackways and bones are common in some Australian Pleistocene deposits.
diprotodon.range: Much of Pleistocene Australia, in woodland, grassland, and around waterholes.
diprotodon.story: Diprotodon is one of the genera that vanish in the ~50,000-40,000-year window after human arrival in Australia. It did not survive to the Last Glacial Maximum. Hunting, fire, and climate are all argued. As with other Sahul megafauna, the honest summary is coincidence with first people plus a climate that was already variable: not a cartoon of total faunal wipeout.
diprotodon.humanRole: Central in the timing; climate is a discussed co-cause. Neither is a sole proven verdict for every site.
diprotodon.sourcesNote: Roberts et al. 2001; later Diprotodon and Australian megafauna chronologies.

haast-eagle.hook: The largest eagle known; it hunted moa, then vanished when people removed its prey.
haast-eagle.imageAlt: Illustration of a Haast’s eagle striking a giant moa in a New Zealand landscape
haast-eagle.what: Haast’s eagle (Hieraaetus moorei, formerly Harpagornis) was the largest eagle on record, perhaps 10-15 kilograms, with talons built to kill moa. It is extinct. Ancient DNA places it with small Australasian Hieraaetus hawks, secondarily gigantic.
haast-eagle.range: South Island of New Zealand. It did not occur on the North Island in the same form.
haast-eagle.story: Polynesian settlers arrived in the thirteenth century and hunted moa out within about 150-200 years. The eagle, specialised on that prey, went with them around the fifteenth century. Eagle bones in middens show people also took the bird itself. Two nineteenth-century sighting claims are not accepted.
haast-eagle.when: Extinct by about the 1400s, with the moa.
haast-eagle.humanRole: Prey extinction after human hunting, plus some direct killing: a clear island chain, not a climate event.
haast-eagle.sourcesNote: Holdaway and later moa-extinction chronologies; Bunce et al. 2005 (ancient DNA); NZ Birds Online.

elephant-bird.hook: Madagascar’s giant flightless birds, hunted and robbed of eggs after people settled the island.
elephant-bird.imageAlt: Historical museum photograph of an elephant-bird skeleton standing beside a huge egg
elephant-bird.what: Elephant birds were giant flightless palaeognaths unique to Madagascar. This entry uses Aepyornis maximus as the face of the group (Vorombe titan, named in 2018, is often treated as the same large form). All are extinct. Their eggs were the largest of any bird.
elephant-bird.range: Madagascar only. Subfossils and eggshells come from the south and centre in particular.
elephant-bird.story: People reached Madagascar in the late Holocene (arrival dates are still argued; often placed within the last two thousand years). Cut and burnt eggshells and hunted bone show harvest. Radiocarbon syntheses put extinction of the large forms around 1000-1200 CE. Later traveller tales of living giants are weak. Habitat clearing and hunting are the main cited causes; climate is sometimes added, not as a replacement for people.
elephant-bird.when: Extinct around 1000-1200 CE, after human settlement: not a deep-time fossil.
elephant-bird.humanRole: Hunting and egg collecting on an island whose giant birds had no prior human predators.
elephant-bird.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Aepyornis maximus, EX); eggshell and bone dating syntheses (Hansford, Crowley, and later).

carolina-parakeet.hook: The only parrot of the eastern United States; the last captive bird died in 1918, in the same zoo as the last passenger pigeon.
carolina-parakeet.imageAlt: A museum mount of a Carolina parakeet, green with an orange-yellow head
carolina-parakeet.what: The Carolina parakeet was a small, social parrot of eastern North American forests and river woods. IUCN lists it as Extinct. It ate seeds and orchard fruit and nested in tree cavities.
carolina-parakeet.range: From the Ohio and Mississippi valleys to Florida and the Gulf coast. It was the northernmost wild parrot in the United States.
carolina-parakeet.story: Forest clearance and shooting as a crop pest destroyed flocks through the nineteenth century. The last widely accepted wild birds were gone by the early 1900s. Incas, the last captive, died on 21 February 1918 at the Cincinnati Zoo: four years after Martha, the last passenger pigeon, in the same building. Disease from poultry is sometimes suggested as a contributing cause.
carolina-parakeet.humanRole: Habitat destruction and persecution as a pest: a documented historical extinction.
carolina-parakeet.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Conuropsis carolinensis, EX); Cincinnati Zoo record for Incas.

falkland-islands-wolf.hook: The only native land mammal of the Falklands; Darwin saw it, and settlers finished it in 1876.
falkland-islands-wolf.imageAlt: Taxidermy of a Falkland Islands wolf, a fox-like canid with a thick brown coat
falkland-islands-wolf.what: The Falkland Islands wolf, or warrah (Dusicyon australis), was a fox-sized canid unique to the Falklands. IUCN lists it as Extinct. It was not a true wolf; its closest relatives are South American foxes. It is the only native terrestrial mammal the islands are known to have had.
falkland-islands-wolf.range: East and West Falkland only. It did not occur on the South American mainland in historic time.
falkland-islands-wolf.story: Charles Darwin, visiting in 1834, wrote that the animal’s tameness would cause its extinction. Settlers shot and poisoned it for fur and as a supposed threat to sheep. The last recorded animal was killed in 1876 at Shallow Bay, West Falkland. No introduced replacement fills the niche.
falkland-islands-wolf.humanRole: Colonial hunting and poisoning: a clear, dated island extinction.
falkland-islands-wolf.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Dusicyon australis, EX); Darwin’s 1834 account; 1876 last-kill record.

bluebuck.hook: The first large African mammal wiped out in historical time: gone from the Cape around 1800.
bluebuck.imageAlt: Taxidermy of a bluebuck, a grey-brown antelope with long ridged horns, in a museum
bluebuck.what: The bluebuck, or blue antelope (Hippotragus leucophaeus), was a relative of the roan and sable, confined to the southwestern Cape. IUCN lists it as Extinct. A bluish sheen on the coat gave the name; few mounted skins survive.
bluebuck.range: A small strip of the Cape Floristic Region, South Africa. Even at European contact the range was already limited.
bluebuck.story: Dutch and later settlers hunted it and converted grazing to livestock. The last animals were taken around 1799-1800. It is generally called the first large African mammal driven to extinction by colonial hunting. Pre-colonial hunting and a naturally small range likely made the end faster; the documented last step is settler overkill.
bluebuck.humanRole: Colonial hunting and pasture conversion of a species already restricted to a small Cape range.
bluebuck.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Hippotragus leucophaeus, EX); Lichtenstein and later historical compilations; South African mammal Red List assessments.

pyrenean-ibex.hook: A Pyrenean subspecies of Iberian ibex; the last wild female died in 2000. A clone born in 2003 lived minutes.
pyrenean-ibex.imageAlt: Taxidermy of a Pyrenean ibex standing in profile against a white background
pyrenean-ibex.what: The Pyrenean ibex, or bucardo (Capra pyrenaica pyrenaica), was a subspecies of Iberian ibex. IUCN treats the subspecies as Extinct. Other subspecies still live in Spain. It is not the Alpine ibex (Capra ibex).
pyrenean-ibex.range: The Pyrenees of Spain and France, historically also neighbouring ranges. By the late twentieth century only a handful remained in Ordesa, Spain.
pyrenean-ibex.story: Centuries of hunting reduced the bucardo to a tiny isolated group. The last wild individual, a female named Celia, was found dead on 6 January 2000. In 2003 a cloned kid was born and died within minutes: the first extinct taxon briefly returned, then lost again. The living Iberian ibex is a different subspecies, not a resurrection.
pyrenean-ibex.when: Extinct in the wild, 2000. The 2003 clone did not survive.
pyrenean-ibex.humanRole: Long hunting pressure, then a population too small to recover: a dated subspecies extinction.
pyrenean-ibex.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Capra pyrenaica pyrenaica, EX, 2008); Ordesa record of Celia, 2000; Folch et al. 2009 cloning paper.

japanese-sea-lion.hook: Hunted out of the Sea of Japan; last reliable colony counted in the 1950s.
japanese-sea-lion.imageAlt: 1934 photograph of Japanese sea lions on a rock at Takeshima
japanese-sea-lion.what: The Japanese sea lion (Zalophus japonicus) was an eared seal of the northwest Pacific, once treated as a subspecies of the California sea lion. IUCN lists it as Extinct. Adult males were large, dark animals of rocky breeding islands.
japanese-sea-lion.range: Coasts of the Japanese archipelago, the Korean Peninsula, and nearby islands, including Takeshima/Dokdo (Liancourt Rocks).
japanese-sea-lion.story: Commercial hunting for oil, skins, and whiskers cut harvests from thousands a year around 1900 to a few dozen by the 1930s. A survey in the 1950s found only about 50-60 animals on Takeshima. A 1974 capture off Hokkaido is often cited as the last record and is also disputed (possible misidentification). Unconfirmed later sightings were not accepted. IUCN assesses the species as Extinct.
japanese-sea-lion.when: Extinct. Last widely accepted colony: 1950s. Possible last record 1974.
japanese-sea-lion.humanRole: Industrial hunting: a twentieth-century marine-mammal extinction.
japanese-sea-lion.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Zalophus japonicus, EX); Japanese harvest statistics; 1950s Takeshima counts.

kauai-oo.hook: The last Hawaiian honeyeater; a lone male was recorded singing in 1987, answering no mate.
kauai-oo.imageAlt: Museum specimen of a Kauaʻi ʻōʻō, a dark honeyeater with yellow thigh tufts
kauai-oo.what: The Kauaʻi ʻōʻō (Moho braccatus) was a forest honeyeater endemic to Kauaʻi, and the last surviving species of Mohoidae: an entire songbird family now gone. IUCN lists it as Extinct. It was not a Hawaiian honeycreeper.
kauai-oo.range: Kauaʻi only, once widespread in native forest, later confined to the Alakaʻi Plateau.
kauai-oo.story: Polynesian rats, later cats, pigs, and especially mosquitoes carrying avian malaria and pox, plus logging, emptied the lowlands. The last confirmed sighting was in 1985; the last recording, a male in 1987. Surveys through 2000 found none. The U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service declared it extinct and delisted it in 2023.
kauai-oo.when: Extinct. Last recording 1987; IUCN EX; U.S. ESA delisting 2023.
kauai-oo.humanRole: Introduced predators and mosquito-borne disease in a forest already cut and fragmented.
kauai-oo.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Moho braccatus, EX); USFWS 2023 delisting; Alakaʻi survey record, 1987.

bramble-cay-melomys.hook: A rodent of one tiny coral cay: the first mammal extinction widely attributed to human-caused climate change.
bramble-cay-melomys.imageAlt: A Bramble Cay melomys on succulent plants and coral sand
bramble-cay-melomys.what: The Bramble Cay melomys (Melomys rubicola) was a mosaic-tailed rat living only on Bramble Cay, a four-hectare coral islet in Torres Strait, Australia. IUCN lists it as Extinct. It ate herbaceous plants on a cay only a few metres above the sea.
bramble-cay-melomys.range: Bramble Cay alone. No other island held a population.
bramble-cay-melomys.story: The last confirmed animal was seen in 2009. A thorough 2014 search found none; Queensland declared the species extinct in 2016. Repeated inundation and storm surge had stripped the vegetation that was its food and cover. Researchers (Woinarski, Waller, and others) identified anthropogenic sea-level rise as the main driver: the first mammal extinction widely assigned to climate change. Honesty still requires the other fact: a species confined to one wash-over cay was already extremely vulnerable.
bramble-cay-melomys.when: Extinct. Last seen 2009; formal declarations 2016 (Queensland) and IUCN EX.
bramble-cay-melomys.humanRole: Climate-driven loss of a tiny island habitat: not hunting. The small range made the climate impact fatal.
bramble-cay-melomys.sourcesNote: IUCN Red List (Melomys rubicola, EX); GBRMPA/Queensland 2016 report; Woinarski and Waller analyses of climate-driven extinction.

huia.hook: A New Zealand forest bird whose male and female had completely different bills.
huia.imageAlt: Old colour plate of a male and a female huia, black birds with orange wattles and white tipped tails
huia.what: The huia (Heteralocha acutirostris) was a large black wattlebird of the North Island of New Zealand. The male had a short, strong bill and the female a long, curved one. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists it as Extinct.
huia.range: Forests of the southern North Island of New Zealand.
huia.story: Māori prized its white tipped tail feathers, worn only by people of high rank. After European settlement, collectors and museums bought skins and feathers, while introduced rats, cats and stoats raided the birds.
huia.humanRole: Introduced predators and, to a lesser degree, hunting for skins and feathers drove it to extinction.

laughing-owl.hook: A New Zealand owl named for its loud call, often compared to a person laughing.
laughing-owl.imageAlt: Old black and white photograph of a live laughing owl perched among ferns
laughing-owl.what: The laughing owl (Sceloglaux albifacies) was a large owl found only in New Zealand. It hunted mostly on the ground, catching insects, lizards, birds and later introduced rats. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists it as Extinct.
laughing-owl.range: Open rocky country of the South Island and Stewart Island, New Zealand.
laughing-owl.story: It was still common when Europeans arrived, but grew rare by 1880. Collectors took many birds and eggs, farming changed the land, and stoats and cats brought in to control rabbits preyed on the owls.
laughing-owl.when: Last confirmed bird found dead in 1914.
laughing-owl.humanRole: Collecting, changes in land use and introduced cats and stoats drove it to extinction.

rodrigues-solitaire.hook: A tall, flightless cousin of the dodo that fought with bony knobs on its wings.
rodrigues-solitaire.imageAlt: Old black and white engraving of a Rodrigues solitaire standing beside a fruiting tree
rodrigues-solitaire.what: The Rodrigues solitaire (Pezophaps solitaria) was a large flightless pigeon from the island of Rodrigues in the Indian Ocean, a close relative of the dodo. Males were much larger than females. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists it as Extinct.
rodrigues-solitaire.range: Rodrigues, a small island east of Mauritius.
rodrigues-solitaire.story: The French traveller François Leguat described it in the 1690s, including how the birds defended their territory with knobs on their wings. Settlers and sailors ate it, and introduced cats and pigs took eggs and chicks.
rodrigues-solitaire.when: Extinct by the late eighteenth century.
rodrigues-solitaire.humanRole: Hunting by people and by animals they brought to the island wiped it out.

cuban-macaw.hook: A small red, orange and yellow macaw that lived only in Cuba.
cuban-macaw.imageAlt: Watercolour from about 1800 of a Cuban macaw, a red parrot with yellow and blue feathers
cuban-macaw.what: The Cuban macaw (Ara tricolor) was one of the smallest macaws, with a red head, orange underside and blue wings. It lived on Cuba and the Isle of Youth. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists it as Extinct.
cuban-macaw.range: Cuba and the Isle of Youth, especially swampy lowlands such as the Zapata Swamp.
cuban-macaw.story: It was hunted and traded by Native Americans and later by Europeans. Hunting for food and the pet trade, together with forest clearing, made it rare by the middle of the nineteenth century.
cuban-macaw.when: Last reliable records in the 1850s on Cuba and 1864 on the Isle of Youth.
cuban-macaw.humanRole: Hunting, the bird trade and destruction of its forests drove it to extinction.

red-rail.hook: A flightless reddish bird of Mauritius that sailors could catch by waving a red cloth.
red-rail.imageAlt: Old colour plate of a red rail, a reddish brown flightless bird with a long curved bill
red-rail.what: The red rail (Aphanapteryx bonasia) was a flightless rail about the size of a chicken, with reddish brown, hair like feathers and a long, curved bill. It lived only on Mauritius. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists it as Extinct.
red-rail.story: Visitors wrote that the birds were attracted to red objects and could be caught easily. Sailors and settlers ate them, and the rats, cats and pigs they brought took the rest.
red-rail.humanRole: Hunting by people and introduced animals drove it to extinction.

hawaii-mamo.hook: A black and gold honeycreeper whose feathers covered the cloaks of Hawaiian kings.
hawaii-mamo.imageAlt: Mounted Hawaiʻi mamo in a museum, a black bird with yellow patches and a long curved bill
hawaii-mamo.what: The Hawaiʻi mamo (Drepanis pacifica) was a black honeycreeper with bright yellow feathers on the rump and thighs and a long, curved bill for drinking nectar. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists it as Extinct.
hawaii-mamo.range: Forests of the island of Hawaiʻi.
hawaii-mamo.story: Hawaiian bird catchers took its yellow feathers for royal cloaks, often releasing the birds. Later, shotgun hunting by collectors, forest clearing, mosquitoes carrying bird diseases and introduced mongooses finished it.
hawaii-mamo.humanRole: Loss of forest, introduced mosquitoes and predators, and heavy hunting for feathers drove it to extinction.

toolache-wallaby.hook: Possibly the most graceful and fastest of all wallabies, gone within 85 years of European settlement.
toolache-wallaby.imageAlt: Old colour plate by John Gould of two toolache wallabies, slender grey kangaroos with banded tails
toolache-wallaby.what: The toolache wallaby (Macropus greyi) was a slender grey wallaby with a banded tail from southeastern Australia. It was famous for its speed and could outrun dogs. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists it as Extinct.
toolache-wallaby.range: Grassy plains and swamps of southeastern South Australia and southwestern Victoria.
toolache-wallaby.story: Settlers drained the swamps and cleared its grasslands, hunted it for sport and for its fur, and brought in the red fox. A rescue attempt in the 1920s went wrong, and most of the last captured animals died.
toolache-wallaby.when: Last wild sightings in 1924, last captive animal died in 1939.
toolache-wallaby.humanRole: Habitat clearing, hunting for sport and fur, and introduced foxes drove it to extinction.

chinese-paddlefish.hook: One of the largest freshwater fish in the world, with a long sword shaped snout.
chinese-paddlefish.imageAlt: Preserved Chinese paddlefish in a museum, a long grey fish with a pointed snout
chinese-paddlefish.what: The Chinese paddlefish (Psephurus gladius) was a giant fish of the Yangtze River that could grow longer than 3 metres. It used its long snout to sense prey in murky water. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists it as Extinct.
chinese-paddlefish.range: The Yangtze and Yellow River basins in China.
chinese-paddlefish.story: The Gezhouba Dam, built in 1981, cut the fish off from its spawning grounds upstream. Overfishing had already reduced the population, and the last live fish was seen in 2003.
chinese-paddlefish.when: Last seen alive in 2003; declared extinct in 2022.
chinese-paddlefish.humanRole: A dam that blocked its migration, together with overfishing, drove it to extinction.

atitlan-grebe.hook: A large, almost flightless grebe that lived on a single volcanic lake in Guatemala.
atitlan-grebe.imageAlt: Mounted Atitlán grebe in a museum, a dark brown diving bird with a thick pale bill
atitlan-grebe.what: The Atitlán grebe (Podilymbus gigas) was a large diving bird with very short wings, found only on Lake Atitlán. Local people called it the poc. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists it as Extinct.
atitlan-grebe.range: Lake Atitlán, in the highlands of Guatemala.
atitlan-grebe.story: Black bass were released into the lake for sport fishing in 1958 and 1960. They ate the young grebes and the crabs and fish the birds lived on, while reed cutting, building on the shore and an earthquake that lowered the lake took the rest.
atitlan-grebe.when: The last two birds were seen in 1989.
atitlan-grebe.humanRole: Fish introduced for angling, reed cutting and shore development drove it to extinction.

choiseul-pigeon.hook: A crested ground pigeon from the Solomon Islands known only from six birds and one egg.
choiseul-pigeon.imageAlt: Old colour plate of a Choiseul pigeon, a blue grey pigeon with a fan shaped crest
choiseul-pigeon.what: The Choiseul pigeon (Microgoura meeki) was a ground living pigeon with a flat, fan like blue crest. It is known only from the six birds and one egg collected in 1904. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists it as Extinct.
choiseul-pigeon.range: Choiseul Island, in the Solomon Islands.
choiseul-pigeon.story: Local people remembered it as a tasty bird that roosted near the ground. Cats brought to the island hunted it, since it had never met a meat eating mammal before.
choiseul-pigeon.humanRole: Cats introduced by people drove it to extinction.

lord-howe-swamphen.hook: A white, flightless relative of the takahē known from just two museum skins.
lord-howe-swamphen.imageAlt: Mounted Lord Howe swamphen in a museum, a white bird with a thick red bill
lord-howe-swamphen.what: The Lord Howe swamphen (Porphyrio albus), also called the white swamphen, was a stocky, flightless bird with mostly white feathers and a heavy red bill. Only two skins survive, in Liverpool and Vienna. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists it as Extinct.
lord-howe-swamphen.range: Lord Howe Island, in the Tasman Sea east of Australia.
lord-howe-swamphen.story: Crews of the first ships to visit the island in 1788 found the birds tame and easy to kill. Whalers and sealers who stopped for food probably hunted them out before settlers arrived in 1834.
lord-howe-swamphen.humanRole: Hunting by visiting sailors probably drove it to extinction.

alaotra-grebe.hook: A small diving bird of one lake in Madagascar, lost to fishing nets and introduced fish.
alaotra-grebe.imageAlt: Photo of a mounted Alaotra grebe, a small brown diving bird with a rusty face
alaotra-grebe.what: The Alaotra grebe (Tachybaptus rufolavatus) was a small grebe with short wings that rarely flew far. It lived almost only on Lake Alaotra. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists it as Extinct.
alaotra-grebe.range: Lake Alaotra and nearby lakes in central eastern Madagascar.
alaotra-grebe.story: Farming and rice fields took over the marshes around the lake. Nylon gill nets drowned diving birds, and a predatory fish released into the lake ate them, while the common little grebe that moved in bred with the last survivors.
alaotra-grebe.when: Last confirmed sighting in 1985; declared extinct in 2010.
alaotra-grebe.humanRole: Destruction of its marshes, fishing nets and an introduced fish drove it to extinction.

pig-footed-bandicoot.hook: A small marsupial of the Australian desert with feet like tiny hooves.
pig-footed-bandicoot.imageAlt: Old colour plate of two small long eared marsupials with thin legs
pig-footed-bandicoot.what: The pig footed bandicoot (Chaeropus ecaudatus) was a small, long legged marsupial of inland southern Australia. Its front feet had two working toes that looked like the hooves of a pig. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists it as Extinct.
pig-footed-bandicoot.range: Dry shrublands and grasslands of inland southern Australia.
pig-footed-bandicoot.story: Aboriginal people of the desert knew it well, and their memories helped scientists learn how it lived. Settlers brought sheep and cattle that ate and trampled its shelter, and foxes and cats that hunted it.
pig-footed-bandicoot.when: Reported gone from its last refuge by 1901.
pig-footed-bandicoot.humanRole: Introduced foxes and cats and the damage done by introduced livestock drove it to extinction.

broad-faced-potoroo.hook: A small rat kangaroo of south western Australia, known from only a handful of specimens.
broad-faced-potoroo.imageAlt: Old colour plate of two small grey brown rat kangaroos with short broad faces
broad-faced-potoroo.what: The broad faced potoroo (Potorous platyops) was a small hopping marsupial, about 30 centimetres long without its tail, with a short, wide face. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists it as Extinct.
broad-faced-potoroo.range: Coastal districts of south western Australia.
broad-faced-potoroo.story: Collectors took only a few animals in the 1840s and the 1870s, and almost nothing is known of how it lived. Writers soon after its loss linked its decline to changed fire patterns and to cats brought by settlers.
broad-faced-potoroo.humanRole: Changed bushfire patterns and introduced cats are linked to its decline.

new-zealand-grayling.hook: A river fish of New Zealand that Māori once caught by the basketful.
new-zealand-grayling.imageAlt: Old drawing of a slender silvery fish seen from the side
new-zealand-grayling.what: The New Zealand grayling (Prototroctes oxyrhynchus) was a slender silvery fish, 30 to 45 centimetres long, that spent part of its life in rivers and part at sea. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists it as Extinct.
new-zealand-grayling.range: Rivers and streams across New Zealand.
new-zealand-grayling.story: Māori caught it in great numbers with woven basket traps set in rivers. After European settlement, forest clearing muddied the rivers, fishing increased, and brown and rainbow trout were released from the 1860s.
new-zealand-grayling.humanRole: Introduced trout, which ate it and took its food, together with fishing and damaged rivers, wiped it out.

rocky-mountain-locust.hook: Its swarms once darkened the North American sky, and then it vanished within a few decades.
rocky-mountain-locust.imageAlt: Old engraving of a grasshopper with long wings, seen from the side
rocky-mountain-locust.what: The Rocky Mountain locust (Melanoplus spretus) was a grasshopper of western North America that formed some of the largest insect swarms ever recorded. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists it as Extinct.
rocky-mountain-locust.range: River valleys of the Rocky Mountains, from where swarms spread across the Great Plains of the United States and Canada.
rocky-mountain-locust.story: Between 1873 and 1877 its swarms ate crops across the Great Plains. The insects bred in a few sheltered river valleys, and when settlers ploughed, watered and grazed those valleys, the eggs in the soil were destroyed.
rocky-mountain-locust.humanRole: Ploughing, irrigation and trampling by livestock in its breeding valleys destroyed its eggs.

mauritius-blue-pigeon.hook: A blue, white and red pigeon of Mauritius, tame enough to be caught by hand.
mauritius-blue-pigeon.imageAlt: Museum specimen of a dark blue pigeon with a white head and neck and a red tail
mauritius-blue-pigeon.what: The Mauritius blue pigeon (Alectroenas nitidissimus) was a stout pigeon about 30 centimetres long, dark blue with a silvery white head and neck and a red tail and face. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists it as Extinct.
mauritius-blue-pigeon.range: Forests of Mauritius in the Indian Ocean.
mauritius-blue-pigeon.story: Settlers found it tame and good to eat. During French rule the lowland forests were almost all cut down, and macaques brought to the island raided the forest birds.
mauritius-blue-pigeon.when: Last specimen shot in 1826; probably gone by the 1830s.
mauritius-blue-pigeon.humanRole: Forest clearing, hunting and introduced macaques drove it to extinction.

palaeopropithecus.hook: A giant sloth lemur of Madagascar that hung upside down from branches like a sloth.
palaeopropithecus.imageAlt: Life restoration of a large shaggy lemur hanging from a branch by its long arms and hooked feet
palaeopropithecus.what: Palaeopropithecus ingens was a large lemur of Madagascar, weighing several tens of kilograms, that moved slowly and hung below branches by long arms and hooked hands and feet. The International Union for Conservation of Nature lists it as Extinct.
palaeopropithecus.story: People reached Madagascar about two thousand years ago. Bones of this lemur with butchery marks show it was hunted and eaten, and its slow movement, daytime habits and slow breeding made it an easy target.
palaeopropithecus.when: Possibly as recent as about four hundred years ago.
palaeopropithecus.humanRole: Hunting by people, helped by its slow movement and slow breeding, is blamed for its extinction.

american-mastodon.hook: A shaggy forest relative of elephants that people of the first American cultures hunted.
american-mastodon.imageAlt: Old colour painting of a mastodon with long tusks walking through a forest
american-mastodon.what: The American mastodon (Mammut americanum) was an elephant relative with a long, low body, short legs and long curved tusks, that browsed on trees and shrubs. The International Union for Conservation of Nature gives it no category, because its Red List covers extinctions since the year 1500.
american-mastodon.range: Forests and wetlands across North America, from Alaska to Mexico.
american-mastodon.story: People reached North America near the end of the last ice age. Mastodon bones with cut marks and stone tools show that the first Americans, including people of the Clovis culture, hunted them, while the climate was also changing fast.
american-mastodon.humanRole: Hunting by the first Americans, alongside the changing climate at the end of the ice age, is linked to its extinction.

sources.label: Faith and Surovell 2009, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences

cave-bear.hook: A huge, mostly plant eating bear that slept through the winter in Europe’s caves.
cave-bear.imageAlt: Mounted cave bear skeleton in a cave, seen from the front and side
cave-bear.what: The cave bear (Ursus spelaeus) was a large bear of Europe, bigger than most brown bears, that ate mainly plants and spent its winters in caves. The International Union for Conservation of Nature gives it no category, because its Red List covers extinctions since the year 1500.
cave-bear.range: Europe, from Spain to the Urals, mostly in hilly country with caves.
cave-bear.story: Thousands of cave bear skeletons fill some European caves where the bears died in their winter sleep. Neanderthals and later modern humans also sought out caves to live in, and they used bear bones as tools.
cave-bear.humanRole: Hunting and competition with people for caves are thought to have played a major part in its extinction.
